A CURE FOR ASTHMA

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scientists at Cardiff University and Kings College London have found out what causes asthma and how to switch it off

Summary:
Asthma could be cured within five years after scientists discovered what causes the condition and how to switch it off. In a breakthrough which could change the lives millions of sufferers, researchers at Cardiff University and Kings College London identified which cells cause the airways to narrow when triggered by irritants like pollution. Crucially, drugs already exist which can deactivate the cells. They are known as calcilytics and are used to treat people with osteoporosis.

Further information:
Asthma could be cured within five years after scientists discovered what causes the condition and how to switch it off. In a breakthrough which could change the lives of Britain’s five million sufferers, researchers at Cardiff University and Kings College London identified which cells cause the airways to narrow when triggered by irritants like pollution.
Crucially, drugs already exist which can deactivate the cells. They are known as calcilytics and are used to treat people with osteoporosis.
The scientists are hopeful that in the future asthmatics take the drug to prevent an attack ever happening and ending the need to constantly carry an inhaler.
"Our findings are incredibly exciting," said Professor Daniela Riccardi, from Cardiff University School of Biosciences.
"If we can prove that calcilytics are safe when administered directly to the lung in people, then in five years we could be in a position to treat patients and potentially stop asthma from happening in the first place.”
Asthma is a debilitating long-term condition which can cause coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness. Although inhalers can manage the problem, some people do not respond to current treatments.
• Hundreds of asthma deaths could be prevented
Scientists knew that asthma was caused by inflammation in the small tubes which carry air and out of the lungs, but did not know what was triggering it.
However experiments on mice and human airway tissue found that calcium sensing receptor (CaSR ) cells - which detect changes in the environment - go into overdrive in asthmatics, triggering airway twitching, inflammation, and narrowing.
But when calcilytic drugs are inhaled, it deactivates the cells and stops all symptoms.
Dr Samantha Walker, Director of Research and Policy at Asthma UK, who helped fund the research, said:
"This hugely exciting discovery enables us, for the first time, to tackle the underlying causes of asthma symptoms.
“Five per cent of people with asthma don't respond to current treatments so research breakthroughs could be life changing for hundreds of thousands of people.
"If this research proves successful we may be just a few years away from a new treatment for asthma, and we urgently need further investment to take it further through clinical trials.
“Asthma research is chronically underfunded; there have only been a handful of new treatments developed in the last 50 years so the importance of investment in research like this is absolutely essential."

------------------------------------
A protein associated with bone growth could also trigger asthma
Calcium may be responsible for asthma symptoms
"Asthma cure could be in reach," The Independent reports. Researchers have discovered that protein molecules called calcium-sensing receptors play a pivotal role in asthma. Drugs known to block these proteins already exist.
In asthma, the immune system mistakes harmless substances, such as pollen, as a threat. White blood cells and inflammatory proteins then collect in the airways. The inflammation causes the airways to constrict, leading to the breathing difficulties associated with asthma. This study found these proteins stimulate calcium-sensing receptors, which leads to further inflammation of the airways.
The research used mouse models of asthma and human airway tissue taken from asthmatic and non-asthmatic people. The researchers found increased numbers of these calcium-sensing receptors compared with healthy lung tissue. They concluded that this is one of the reasons for the exaggerated inflammatory response that occurs in asthma.

The drug calcityrol, which is used to treat osteoporosis, is known to block the actions of the receptors. It reduced inflammation of the airways when used in mice.

However, it is not clear that calcityrol could be a "cure" for asthma, as the initial inflammatory response by the immune system would still occur.

Though calcityrol pills are safe as a treatment for osteoporosis, it is not known whether the dose required to be effective in reducing the inflammation found in asthma would be safe.
The researchers plan to develop a version of the drug that can be inhaled to maximise its effectiveness and minimise side effects. They expect human trials to commence in a couple of years.

Where did the story come from?

The study was carried out by researchers from Cardiff University, the Open University, the Mayo Clinic, and the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine in the US, and the University of Manchester and King's College London in the UK.
It was funded by Asthma UK, the Cardiff Partnership Fund, Marie Curie Initial Training Network, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, and the US National Institutes of Health.

Four of the authors report they are co-inventors of a patent for the use of calcium-sensing receptor antagonists for the treatment of inflammatory lung diseases.

The study was published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Translational Medicine.
The media reported the story accurately, although headlines saying that an asthma "cure" is five years away are a little premature. No clinical studies in people have been conducted yet, and there is no guarantee they will work. However, the "five-year cure" claim came from the researchers themselves.

What kind of research was this?

This was a set of laboratory experiments involving mice models of asthma and samples of human lung tissue. The researchers aimed to better understand the inflammation that causes narrowing of the airways in asthma.

The inflammation is an exaggerated response to various triggers, such as pollen, infections and pollutants, but sometimes no cause is identified.

Recent research found that this inflammation results in the build-up of two proteins: eosinophilic cationic protein (ECP) and major basic protein. These proteins carry multiple positive electrical charges.
The researchers wanted to test the theory that the inflammation is driven by these proteins activating another type of protein molecule called calcium-sensing receptors (CaSR) on the surface of the smooth muscle cells that line the airways.
What did the research involve?

The researchers conducted a variety of laboratory experiments, which involved looking at human lung tissue samples taken from people with asthma and comparing them with healthy lung tissue. They then performed several studies comparing mice with a type of asthma with healthy controls.
The researchers first compared the number of CaSRs in the lung tissue of people with asthma, compared with healthy lung tissue. They then measured how the CaSRs reacted to positively charged proteins and various chemicals involved in inflammatory response, such as histamine.
They repeated the experiments using a type of drug called a calcilytic, which blocks CaSRs. Calcilytic drugs were developed as a treatment for osteoporosis, as they increase the level of parathyroid hormone by targeting CaSRs. This helps to increase the level of calcium in the blood.
What were the basic results?

The experiments indicated there are more CaSRs in people with asthma, which are required for inflammation. Calcilytic drugs blocked the receptors.

There were three times the number of CaSRs in biopsies of smooth muscle taken from the airways of people with asthma, compared with those who do not have asthma. The same was true for biopsies of mice with a form of asthma, compared with healthy controls.

In the laboratory setting, positively charged proteins and chemicals such as histamine activated the CaSRs, causing an inflammatory response. These receptors could be blocked by the calcilytic drugs.
Mice without CaSRs in their smooth muscle cells did not have an inflammatory response to the positively charged proteins. Healthy control mice did have an inflammatory response. Calcilytic drugs were able to reduce the effect of these proteins and other inflammatory stimulants tested.
How did the researchers interpret the results?

The researchers concluded that there are more CaSRs in the lungs of people with asthma, and this contributes to the inflammation that causes narrowing of the airways.

They say that calcilytic drugs could reduce the number of CaSRs and reduce their responsiveness. This could both "prevent as well as relieve AHR [airways hyper-responsiveness]", which is found in asthma.


Yarova PL, Stewart AL, Sathish V, et al. Calcium-sensing receptor antagonists abrogate airway hyperresponsiveness and inflammation in allergic asthma. Science Translational Medicine. Published online April 22 2015

Press Release:


A Cure for Asthma
In a remarkable yet accidental discovery, scientists at Cardiff University and Kings College London have found out what causes asthma and how to switch it off. Researchers have identified cells that cause the airways to narrow when triggered by irritants like pollution. Most surprisingly, drugs that could deactivate these cells already exist - ironically to treat people with osteoporosis. Carte Blanche asks if this chance discovery could mean the end of asthma for 300 million sufferers worldwide?


Script:


Wouter:
…..inhaled steroids, you drink some pills. Eventually you take a nebuliser to help. Antihistamines. Maybe some nasal sprays.
V/O:
Wouter Pretorius needs of all these medications on a daily basis to keep functioning. He is an asthmatic and has been living with asthma since childhood.
Wouter:
There is not much that you can do. There is only so much and then that’s it. So you cannot get rid of the condition. It’s there.

Derek:
And steroids seem to be the only way to live with it?

Wouter:
It does not seem like the right way, does it? But you’re right. It’s the only thing you can use to keep it, sort of under control.
V/O:
Wouter has a chronic asthmatic condition which makes his life very difficult.
Wouter:
I would struggle to breathe, lot of phlegm and coughing. And eventually it will go away and there is nothing you can do to it.
Derek:
What would you give to be free of the condition?
Wouter:
There is a lot that I would give. Money, as much as I’ve got I’ll give it.
Link:
Wouter’s sentiments are the sentiments of most asthma sufferers -- to be free of the asthma inhaler forever. But the idea of a cure for the disease has been nothing but a pipe dream. Until now.
V/O:
A cure for asthma may be on the cards, and it has been discovered here at Kings College in London.

Professor Jeremy Ward is one of the UK’s leading asthma researchers.
Jeremy:
Asthma is a problem disease because so many people have symptoms of asthma. They find their quality of life is depressed because they have to use the inhaler. They have to worry about smoke in the air. And of course the very severe asthmatics have much more severe problems than that.
V/O:
It is estimated that about 300 million people worldwide suffer from asthma.
Jeremy:
This number has been growing year on year on year. Prevalence has been increasing and this is particularly the case in westernised societies, developed societies.
LINK:
In South Africa the numbers are very high and there are an estimated 3.9 million asthma sufferers. Up until now the only treatment available was to try and alleviate the symptoms or try and prevent attacks by taking steroids.
V/O:
The effects of asthma on the body are well understood. These are images from a bronchoscopy and this is what healthy lungs look like. The airways are open and air can flow freely in and out of the lungs. Asthma changes this picture.
Jeremy:
People with asthma have very twitchy airways, which is hyper responsiveness. So those airways will respond to things that a person without asthma wouldn’t even notice. A little bit of cigarette smoke in the air, a little bit of one particular type of pollen.
V/O:
So, asthmatics’ lungs react to stimuli that ordinarily don’t affect other people.
Jeremy:
Trouble is they do that inappropriately. It’s at the wrong time to the wrong stimulus. So you get this narrowing of your airways, the wheezing. They can’t breathe, they become panicky. It’s very unpleasant. So all asthmatics are hyper-responsive, hyper-reactive.
V/O:
On the left is a healthy airway, muscles around the airway are relaxed and air can flow easily. Asthma causes the muscles around the airways to begin to constrict. The lining of the airway can become inflamed, narrowing the airway and inhibiting proper airflow.

But one piece of the puzzle has evaded scientists -- the underlying cause of some people’s hyper-responsiveness.
Jeremy:
And that is one of the questions we as asthma researchers have been looking at for many, many years.
V/O:
Jeremy had been friends with Prof Daniela Riccardi for many years. She is a physiologist and never had any interest in asthma. Rather, she focuses on calcium receptors in human cells.
Daniela:
My field of research was this particular sensor and its involvement in the control of calcium metabolism - for instance osteoporosis but also additional diseases such as chronic kidney disease.
LINK:
But then one day after a conference Jeremy and Daniela compared notes. They discovered that if work they had been doing independently were to be combined, they could change the understanding of asthma profoundly.
V/O:
Daniela had found that when calcium receptors in cells are triggered, this would result in increased levels of calcium.

Jeremy and his team had found that there were a surprising number of cells with increased levels of calcium in the lung cells of asthmatics.
Jeremy:
Much more that we would expect and that’s when we thought: “If there’s a lot of it, it must be doing something.”
V/O:
What these cells with increased calcium levels were doing was producing a protein that caused the muscle cells around airways to constrict.

The last remaining piece of the puzzle of asthma’s exact causes had been found – it was oversensitive calcium receptors in lung cells.
Daniela:
And therefore activation of the sensor is responsible for causing our airways to narrow to become particularly hyper-reactive or twitchy, but also to cause inflammation inside the lungs. And that is the first time that there is an established link between cause and effect.
LINK:
So for the first time scientists fully understood the causes of asthma. And this made it possible to find a new way of attacking the disease.
Daniela:
So if we can reduce the levels, the basil levels of calcium inside the cells of the airways smooth muscle, we can reduce the risk of our airways becoming hyper-responsive to any stimulus. And therefore become more normal, if you like.
V/O:
So, if the over-sensitive calcium receptors can be deactivated, this should put a stop to all asthma symptoms.

The next step would be developing a drug to do just this. But to develop such a can take decades and cost hundreds of millions of rands.

Daniela then realized something game-changing. A drug that prevented the triggering of calcium receptors already existed. This drug had been developed to treat osteoporosis.
Daniela
I knew of the results of the clinical trials for osteoporosis that showed that although the drug was safe in patients when it was taken orally. But it did not show any effects and therefore the pharmaceutical company put it on a shelf and left it there.
V/O:
Yet this drug had already undergone human trials and been declared safe.
Jeremy:
It is extremely exciting. It’s the only drug compound we know that actually reduces the twitchiness of the airways. But it does more than that. Because we think that its actually what you might call upstream. Right up close to the actual stimulus that is causing the problem, rather than most of the current treatments that is right down getting rid of the symptoms. It may actually be more effective.
Daniela:
If we can remove the causes, the triggers, then potentially this reduction in our baseline calcium levels inside the cells of the airways, could become a cure for asthma.
LINK:
Because most of the development and approvals of the drug are already in place, Daniela believes that this cure for asthma could be freely available within the next 5 years.
V/O:
So, couple a chance discussion between two scientists working in different fields with the innovative use of a previously ineffective drug and the lives of millions of people around the world could very soon change. And, one of them is Wouter.
Wouter:
It would absolutely be awesome. It would really change my life. It would make a lot of the constant difficulty in breathing, will just take it away. So absolutely awesome and looking forward to such a resolution to this problem.

Jeremy: And that is one of the questions we as asthma researchers have been looking at for many, many years. V/O: Jeremy had been friends with Prof Daniela Riccardi for many years. She is a physiologist and never had any interest in asthma. Rather, she focuses on calcium receptors in human cells. Daniela: My field of research was this particular sensor and its involvement in the control of calcium metabolism - for instance osteoporosis but also additional diseases such as chronic kidney disease. LINK: But then one day after a conference Jeremy and Daniela compared notes. They discovered that if work they had been doing independently were to be combined, they could change the understanding of asthma profoundly. V/O: Daniela had found that when calcium receptors in cells are triggered, this would result in increased levels of calcium. Jeremy and his team had found that there were a surprising number of cells with increased levels of calcium in the lung cells of asthmatics. Jeremy: Much more that we would expect and that’s when we thought: “If there’s a lot of it, it must be doing something.” V/O: What these cells with increased calcium levels were doing was producing a protein that caused the muscle cells around airways to constrict. The last remaining piece of the puzzle of asthma’s exact causes had been found – it was oversensitive calcium receptors in lung cells. Daniela: And therefore activation of the sensor is responsible for causing our airways to narrow to become particularly hyper-reactive or twitchy, but also to cause inflammation inside the lungs. And that is the first time that there is an established link between cause and effect. LINK: So for the first time scientists fully understood the causes of asthma. And this made it possible to find a new way of attacking the disease. Daniela: So if we can reduce the levels, the basil levels of calcium inside the cells of the airways smooth muscle, we can reduce the risk of our airways becoming hyper-responsive to any stimulus. And therefore become more normal, if you like. V/O: So, if the over-sensitive calcium receptors can be deactivated, this should put a stop to all asthma symptoms. The next step would be developing a drug to do just this. But to develop such a can take decades and cost hundreds of millions of rands. Daniela then realized something game-changing. A drug that prevented the triggering of calcium receptors already existed. This drug had been developed to treat osteoporosis. Daniela I knew of the results of the clinical trials for osteoporosis that showed that although the drug was safe in patients when it was taken orally. But it did not show any effects and therefore the pharmaceutical company put it on a shelf and left it there. V/O: Yet this drug had already undergone human trials and been declared safe. Jeremy: It is extremely exciting. It’s the only drug compound we know that actually reduces the twitchiness of the airways. But it does more than that. Because we think that its actually what you might call upstream. Right up close to the actual stimulus that is causing the problem, rather than most of the current treatments that is right down getting rid of the symptoms. It may actually be more effective. Daniela: If we can remove the causes, the triggers, then potentially this reduction in our baseline calcium levels inside the cells of the airways, could become a cure for asthma. LINK: Because most of the development and approvals of the drug are already in place, Daniela believes that this cure for asthma could be freely available within the next 5 years. V/O: So, couple a chance discussion between two scientists working in different fields with the innovative use of a previously ineffective drug and the lives of millions of people around the world could very soon change. And, one of them is Wouter. Wouter: It would absolutely be awesome. It would really change my life. It would make a lot of the constant difficulty in breathing, will just take it away. So absolutely awesome and looking forward to such a resolution to this problem. metadata.Summary: Asthma could be cured within five years after scientists discovered what causes the condition and how to switch it off. metadata.Further information: Asthma could be cured within five years after scientists discovered what causes the condition and how to switch it off. In a breakthrough which could change the lives of Britain’s five million sufferers, researchers at Cardiff University and Kings College London identified which cells cause the airways to narrow when triggered by irritants like pollution. Crucially, drugs already exist which can deactivate the cells. They are known as calcilytics and are used to treat people with osteoporosis. The scientists are hopeful that in the future asthmatics take the drug to prevent an attack ever happening and ending the need to constantly carry an inhaler. "Our findings are incredibly exciting," said Professor Daniela Riccardi, from Cardiff University School of Biosciences. "If we can prove that calcilytics are safe when administered directly to the lung in people, then in five years we could be in a position to treat patients and potentially stop asthma from happening in the first place.” Asthma is a debilitating long-term condition which can cause coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness. Although inhalers can manage the problem, some people do not respond to current treatments. • Hundreds of asthma deaths could be prevented Scientists knew that asthma was caused by inflammation in the small tubes which carry air and out of the lungs, but did not know what was triggering it. However experiments on mice and human airway tissue found that calcium sensing receptor (CaSR ) cells - which detect changes in the environment - go into overdrive in asthmatics, triggering airway twitching, inflammation, and narrowing. But when calcilytic drugs are inhaled, it deactivates the cells and stops all symptoms. Dr Samantha Walker, Director of Research and Policy at Asthma UK, who helped fund the research, said: "This hugely exciting discovery enables us, for the first time, to tackle the underlying causes of asthma symptoms. “Five per cent of people with asthma don't respond to current treatments so research breakthroughs could be life changing for hundreds of thousands of people. "If this research proves successful we may be just a few years away from a new treatment for asthma, and we urgently need further investment to take it further through clinical trials. “Asthma research is chronically underfunded; there have only been a handful of new treatments developed in the last 50 years so the importance of investment in research like this is absolutely essential." ------------------------------------ A protein associated with bone growth could also trigger asthma Calcium may be responsible for asthma symptoms "Asthma cure could be in reach," The Independent reports. Researchers have discovered that protein molecules called calcium-sensing receptors play a pivotal role in asthma. Drugs known to block these proteins already exist. In asthma, the immune system mistakes harmless substances, such as pollen, as a threat. White blood cells and inflammatory proteins then collect in the airways. The inflammation causes the airways to constrict, leading to the breathing difficulties associated with asthma. This study found these proteins stimulate calcium-sensing receptors, which leads to further inflammation of the airways. The research used mouse models of asthma and human airway tissue taken from asthmatic and non-asthmatic people. The researchers found increased numbers of these calcium-sensing receptors compared with healthy lung tissue. They concluded that this is one of the reasons for the exaggerated inflammatory response that occurs in asthma. The drug calcityrol, which is used to treat osteoporosis, is known to block the actions of the receptors. It reduced inflammation of the airways when used in mice. However, it is not clear that calcityrol could be a "cure" for asthma, as the initial inflammatory response by the immune system would still occur. Though calcityrol pills are safe as a treatment for osteoporosis, it is not known whether the dose required to be effective in reducing the inflammation found in asthma would be safe. The researchers plan to develop a version of the drug that can be inhaled to maximise its effectiveness and minimise side effects. They expect human trials to commence in a couple of years. Where did the story come from? The study was carried out by researchers from Cardiff University, the Open University, the Mayo Clinic, and the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine in the US, and the University of Manchester and King's College London in the UK. It was funded by Asthma UK, the Cardiff Partnership Fund, Marie Curie Initial Training Network, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, and the US National Institutes of Health. Four of the authors report they are co-inventors of a patent for the use of calcium-sensing receptor antagonists for the treatment of inflammatory lung diseases. The study was published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Translational Medicine. The media reported the story accurately, although headlines saying that an asthma "cure" is five years away are a little premature. No clinical studies in people have been conducted yet, and there is no guarantee they will work. However, the "five-year cure" claim came from the researchers themselves. What kind of research was this? This was a set of laboratory experiments involving mice models of asthma and samples of human lung tissue. The researchers aimed to better understand the inflammation that causes narrowing of the airways in asthma. The inflammation is an exaggerated response to various triggers, such as pollen, infections and pollutants, but sometimes no cause is identified. Recent research found that this inflammation results in the build-up of two proteins: eosinophilic cationic protein (ECP) and major basic protein. These proteins carry multiple positive electrical charges. The researchers wanted to test the theory that the inflammation is driven by these proteins activating another type of protein molecule called calcium-sensing receptors (CaSR) on the surface of the smooth muscle cells that line the airways. What did the research involve? The researchers conducted a variety of laboratory experiments, which involved looking at human lung tissue samples taken from people with asthma and comparing them with healthy lung tissue. They then performed several studies comparing mice with a type of asthma with healthy controls. The researchers first compared the number of CaSRs in the lung tissue of people with asthma, compared with healthy lung tissue. They then measured how the CaSRs reacted to positively charged proteins and various chemicals involved in inflammatory response, such as histamine. They repeated the experiments using a type of drug called a calcilytic, which blocks CaSRs. Calcilytic drugs were developed as a treatment for osteoporosis, as they increase the level of parathyroid hormone by targeting CaSRs. This helps to increase the level of calcium in the blood. What were the basic results? The experiments indicated there are more CaSRs in people with asthma, which are required for inflammation. Calcilytic drugs blocked the receptors. There were three times the number of CaSRs in biopsies of smooth muscle taken from the airways of people with asthma, compared with those who do not have asthma. The same was true for biopsies of mice with a form of asthma, compared with healthy controls. In the laboratory setting, positively charged proteins and chemicals such as histamine activated the CaSRs, causing an inflammatory response. These receptors could be blocked by the calcilytic drugs. Mice without CaSRs in their smooth muscle cells did not have an inflammatory response to the positively charged proteins. Healthy control mice did have an inflammatory response. Calcilytic drugs were able to reduce the effect of these proteins and other inflammatory stimulants tested. How did the researchers interpret the results? The researchers concluded that there are more CaSRs in the lungs of people with asthma, and this contributes to the inflammation that causes narrowing of the airways. They say that calcilytic drugs could reduce the number of CaSRs and reduce their responsiveness. This could both "prevent as well as relieve AHR [airways hyper-responsiveness]", which is found in asthma. Yarova PL, Stewart AL, Sathish V, et al. Calcium-sensing receptor antagonists abrogate airway hyperresponsiveness and inflammation in allergic asthma. Science Translational Medicine. Published online April 22 2015
